lede: Cooler PCE cuts October hike odds to 35%; the 10-year still closes at its highest since 2002.
geo_headlines: INFLATION CAME IN COOLER THAN FEARED. August PCE prices rose 3.4% from a year ago against 3.7% expected; core was 3.0% against 3.3%, with core up 0.2% on the month (CNBC). **Spending still rose 0.9%, so this was not a weak consumer.** Part of the miss reflects BEA measurement changes that lowered the July core level. Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% (BEA).

OCTOBER HIKE ODDS FELL AGAIN, TO 35%. FedWatch now puts an October 28 hike at 35.4%, down from 46.5% a day earlier and about 70% on Monday; a December hike is 87.7% priced. The market has moved the next hike from October to December.

AND LONG YIELDS STILL ROSE. Treasury's curve: the 10-year closed at 5.29% (+3bp), its highest since May 2002; the 30-year at 5.64% (+5bp), the highest published 30-year close since July 2001. The 2-year slipped to 4.88%, so the 2s10s curve steepened to 41bp. The 10-year TIPS yield rose 2bp to 2.93%. Japan's 10-year rose 6bp to 3.11% overnight (Bloomberg).

STOCKS GAVE UP A PCE RALLY INTO THE CLOSE. The S&P 500 closed down 0.25% at 7,651.54, at its session low, after trading up about 0.4% in the morning; the Dow fell 444 points and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.23%. The S&P is 1.89% below its August 13 record and the Nasdaq 100 1.05% below its September 22 record. VIX 16.34.

MICRON BEAT, AND FUTURES ARE LEANING ON IT. Micron reported fiscal Q4 revenue of $54.23 billion against about $50.45 billion expected and adjusted EPS of $33.42 against $31.16, and said AI memory demand stays tight through 2028; the stock was little changed after hours (Investing.com). Nasdaq futures +0.77%, S&P futures +0.35%; Japan's Nikkei closed up 3.3% and Korea's Kospi 2.0% on chips (AP).

IRAN RECEIVED A US COUNTERPROPOSAL; OIL BACK TO $100. Iran's cabinet is weighing the US response; Reuters says the sides largely agree on steps but not their order. Two ships were hit by projectiles Tuesday (UKMTO via Reuters). Brent December is $100.00 (+2.0%) and WTI $91.73 (+1.5%). Europe opened lower: the Stoxx 600 fell 1% (Reuters), with the FTSE down 1.8% early (AP).

TODAY: ISM, TWO FED SPEAKERS, NIKE. Jobless claims at 8:30 AM; ISM manufacturing and construction spending at 10:00; Governor Waller at 10:00 and Vice Chair Jefferson at 1:30 PM. Nike, McCormick and Accenture report. Friday's September payrolls are expected around 85,000 with unemployment at 4.1%.
client_frame_short: Yesterday brought good news on inflation: the Fed's preferred gauge came in well below forecasts, and markets now see the next rate hike in December rather than October. **Yet the 10-year Treasury yield still rose to its highest close since 2002, which tells you long rates are being driven by more than the Fed.** Stocks dipped slightly, and futures are higher this morning on strong Micron results. Nothing here calls for action; yields near 5% remain an opportunity for idle cash, and Friday's jobs report is the next real test.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, lead with the good news, then explain why it did not lower their mortgage rate.

The good news: inflation cooled more than expected in August. The Fed's preferred measure rose 3.4% from a year ago, against forecasts of 3.7%, and the core measure that strips out food and energy came in at 3.0%. Consumer spending still grew strongly, up 0.9% in the month, and second-quarter growth was revised up to 2.2%, so this is not a weakening economy. Markets responded sensibly: the chance of another Fed rate hike in October fell to about 35%, from about 70% on Monday.

The puzzle: long-term Treasury yields rose anyway. The 10-year closed at 5.29%, its highest since May 2002, and the 30-year at 5.64%. Short rates follow the Fed and eased. Long rates follow what investors demand to lend for a decade or more, and that is being pushed up by large government deficits, heavy borrowing for AI data centers, rising bond yields abroad, including Japan, and oil back near $100. The 10-year was the trigger we flagged at 5.25%; it is now 5.29%, and it is moving for reasons a softer Fed does not fix.

Stocks are absorbing this better than headlines suggest. The S&P 500 slipped 0.25% Wednesday and sits 1.89% below its August 13 record; Micron's strong results, with revenue well ahead of forecasts and AI memory demand described as tight through 2028, have Nasdaq futures up this morning.

For clients, the practical message is unchanged: high-quality bonds now pay real returns not seen in two decades, which is an opportunity for income and idle cash, and equity portfolios built for the long run do not need changing for a yield move. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40%, a 30-year above 5.75%, or a strong payrolls report Friday that puts October hike odds back above 50%.
